title: Writing a Simple Grant Application in Canada
summary: By the end, learners can tell a grant from other kinds of government support, find official program lists (including Innovation Canada’s Business Benefits Finder and Alberta’s non-profit grant pages), read eligibility and expense rules before they write, gather common documents, write clear and honest answers to the questions asked, and describe what happens after they apply — without treating this course as a consultant licence or a guarantee of funding.

lessons.title: Know what you are applying for
lessons.html:
This course is for people who help a community group, council, or small organization look at government funding in Canada. It also helps if you support a small business that wants to search official programs. It does not promise that you will receive money. Finishing the course does not make you a paid grant consultant.

Government support is not only “a grant.” Innovation Canada’s Business Benefits Finder groups many kinds of help. A grant is money you may not have to repay if you follow the program’s rules. Other supports can include loans (money you repay), tax credits, wage subsidies, chances to work with researchers, and expert advice. The right tool depends on your project and on who you are. A registered non-profit is not the same as a for-profit business.

The Government of Alberta says there is work to do before you even start completing a grant application. Innovation Canada asks you to check fit first:

  • Is this project already part of your 12-to-24-month plan?
  • Would you still do the work without the funding?
  • Do you have the people and time to deliver the project and report on it?
  • Are you applying because the program fits, or only because the money exists?

Processing can take weeks or months. If you need to start tomorrow, a slow program may not be the right match. Innovation Canada also notes that government funding is designed to share risk, not to pay every cost. Many business programs expect the applicant to contribute, and asking for 100% of the costs is often a non-starter. That is a general tip for business funding, not a rule for every community grant. Always read the live program page.

lessons.title: Find official programs
lessons.html:
Start on official government sites. Do not pay a random website for a “secret list” of grants.

Innovation Canada describes the Business Benefits Finder as the place to get a tailored list of what government can do for a business. As of November 2026, its how-to page said the Finder brings together more than 1,500 federal, provincial, and territorial supports, then narrows them after you answer questions. Check the live page; that number can change.

To get better results:

  • Answer in detail. Choose “not sure” only when you truly do not know.
  • Think about your goal.
  • After you complete a “story,” filter to programs that are currently accepting applications.
  • View results by category or as a list.
  • Use Share to email the list. Innovation Canada says the shared list stays up to date when you open it again.
  • You can also start from all programs and use filters or a keyword search.
  • Save your story and sign up for email notices. You can favourite a program to hear when a deadline is coming.

This course could not open the Finder’s separate start address this session. Begin at the official Innovation Canada website and follow the Business Benefits Finder link there.

Canada.ca’s page on getting business support and financing also points you to the Finder. For Alberta it lists Prairies Economic Development Canada, the Prairies Business Service Network, and Community Futures Alberta.

If you help a charity or non-profit in Alberta, use Alberta.ca’s hub for grants, funding, and supports for non-profits, and the page on preparing and applying for grants. That page points to training such as Grant Writing 101 — open it there rather than copying a webinar.

lessons.title: Read the guidelines before you write
lessons.html:
Innovation Canada says many applications are rejected because the organization or the project expenses are not eligible. Before you write, read who can apply, what costs are eligible, any limits, and matching rules. If you still have questions, call a program officer. Do not invent a rule that is not on the page.

This is how to read a live program page — an example, not a promise of funding.

As of November 2026, Alberta’s Community Initiatives Program (CIP) Project Grant page said funding can be up to $75,000 for certain community-driven initiatives, programs, and events. The next intake deadline listed there was February 15, 2027. The program is moving to two intakes each year (February 15 and August 15), and review takes about six months. Check the live CIP page; those figures and dates can change.

Eligible applicants were Alberta-based non-profits registered and in good standing under named acts, operational for at least one full year, able to provide a financial statement for that year, and with an Alberta address that an active member monitors. Municipalities, for-profits, individuals, schools (as defined on that page), and organizations with overdue ministry-grant reporting were listed as ineligible.

CIP Project funding is approved only on a matching basis: the applicant must contribute an amount equal to or exceeding the amount requested, plus any remaining funds needed. Total Government of Alberta funding cannot exceed 50% of total project costs. Those matching rules are not true for every grant in Canada.

Applications go through the GATE Front Office portal. Registration can take up to 10 business days, so register at least 10 business days before a deadline. Email the form to registration.cg@gov.ab.ca and choose Community Grants as the program area. For in-kind matching, use only the donated-labour rates printed on the live CIP page.

lessons.title: Write clear, honest answers
lessons.html:
When you write, Innovation Canada’s experts say: avoid marketing language. These programs are funded by Canadian taxpayers, so officers need a clear picture they can explain to someone who does not know your work. Use everyday words. Say what you will do, who will benefit, and how you will know it worked.

Answer the questions that are asked. After a long writing session it is easy to describe your whole organization and forget the question. Have a colleague read the draft and check that each question has a direct answer. Innovation Canada also says less is more: give what they ask for so every applicant is judged on the same information.

Prepare common documents early. Innovation Canada notes that many business applications ask for a description of the organization, the number of employees, the past three years of financial statements, and incorporation documents. For a project they often want a description, a detailed expense breakdown, risks, and the benefits for Canada. Keep a folder of facts you can reuse — then tailor the last part to this program. Do not copy and paste without updating.

Alberta’s CIP Project page (as of November 2026) shows how specific a document list can be: a board member list with positions and contacts; recent financial statements signed by two signing authorities; current bank statement(s); a signed grant agreement from the portal; an Application for Electronic Payment and a void cheque; and quotes or estimates for project costs. Other items apply only in some cases, such as letters for donated in-kind support. Incomplete applications will not be accepted.

Use honest numbers. If you need help writing short, plain sentences, see the LearnHere course on workplace writing and grammar. This lesson is not Outlook or email training.

lessons.title: After you apply
lessons.html:
Sending the form is not the end of the work.

Innovation Canada warns that reporting can take more time than people expect. In many business programs, money is reimbursed through claims, sometimes monthly or quarterly, and some reporting can continue after the project ends. Factor that work into your plan before you apply. Rules differ by program — read yours.

On Alberta’s CIP Project page (as of November 2026):

  • Incomplete applications are not accepted.
  • Decisions are final and there is no appeal.
  • Notification is emailed to the contacts on the application, about six months after the intake deadline.
  • If you are declined, you may submit a new application for the same project if you have not already incurred the expenses.
  • If you receive a grant, the project must be completed and fully reported within 18 months of the grant payment date, unless an extension is approved.

Newer CIP applications submitted through GATE Front Office report in that portal. Older awards follow the instructions on the live page.

Keep copies of what you sent, any emails, and the guidelines that were posted when you applied.

For CIP questions, Alberta’s Community Grants office listed these contacts: 780-422-9598, toll free 1-800-642-3855, and communitygrants@gov.ab.ca, weekdays from 8:15 am to 4:00 pm (closed statutory holidays).

A clear application improves your chance of a fair review. It does not guarantee funding. Check the live program page before every new intake.

keptBack.sourceDisclaimer: This course is general information about finding official grant and funding pages in Canada and reading them before you write. It is not a promise that you or your organization will receive money. It is not a grant-consultant credential, not legal, tax, or financial advice, and not a substitute for a program’s own guidelines. Grant amounts, deadlines, and rules change. Always check the live official page before you apply.
